newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurobourses slip from record highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurobourses slip from record highs.

text.p: Leading British and German shares scored early record highs but later retreated in relatively quiet European trading on Monday, the ninth anniversary of the 1987 "Black Monday" crash.
By mid-afternoon London shares were off their peak, uninspired by a softer opening on Wall Street, and Frankfurt ended floor trading lower.

The dollar clung to its highest level against the yen for more than two years. The weekend Japanese election result had effectively weakened the yen by doing little to alter expectations of a continuing easy money policy in Japan.
In Monday afternoon trading in Europe the dollar was holding firm just shy of a 33-month high of 112.86 yen set in early trading.
Overnight, Tokyo stocks had slid sharply while government bonds surged to a record high after the poll, which left the pro-business Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) without a clear majority.

Against the mark the dollar softened to 1.5355 from an early high of 1.5435 after news that German September M3 money supply growth, the Bundesbank's key policy indicator, had slowed. This reinforced opinions that, in the near term at least, the German central bank would not reduce interest rates.

Analysts said the Japanese election result meant it was most likely Tokyo would go ahead with planned sales tax rises in April and modest fiscal tightening would allow the central bank to keep interest rates low.

"The net effect of the polls seems to be that there is really no change at all and a continuation of existing policies will remain yen-negative," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.

Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita underlined the current low interest rate policy when he told a meeting of the bank's regional branch managers that monetary policy was aimed at securing a solid base for economic recovery.

The London Stock Exchange's blue-chip FTSE 100 index hit 4,064.1 in early trading, a rise of 11.0 points to beat its previous best of 4,063.2 set on October 15. Later it dropped back somewhat but remained above Friday's levels.
While the anniversary was passing off relatively quietly, many still remained nervous that corrections in both the British and U.S. markets were overdue.

"We're seeing follow-through from Friday and the market's still fairly frothy. Dealers are saying we're going better but don't be too assured about it. There are one or two things lurking in the background," said one trader.

In early Frankfurt trading the 30-share IBIS DAX index rose 15.91 points to 2,743.47. Its previous peak was 2,739.42, hit on October 18. Later the bourse turned down however and floor trading closed weaker with dealers saying the market was consolidating following its record-breaking run of recent weeks.

The Paris bourse was also weak, trading down after a slightly firmer opening. Dealers said the market was affected by profit-taking after Friday's gains, which saw the main CAC-40 index close at its highest since May 1994.
CURRENCIES AT 1445 GMT
The dollar was trading at 112.77 yen and 1.5355 marks compared with Friday's London close of 112.59 yen and 1.5431 marks.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1445 GMT
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares had risen 6.8 points to 4,059.9.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index dropped 3.38 to 2,181.4.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 5.79 at 2,729.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $381.00 compared with Friday's $380.15 London close. Silver was up two cents at $4.94.
